title: Job again
hook: God never explains, but shows up, and Job's friends are rebuked

segments.voice: Yesterday, theodicy: the question of suffering, if God is good. Your line was no easy answers. Did you catch a quick explanation before it left your mouth? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-eight.

The casseroles arrive first. Then the cards. Then, sooner or later, the explanations. Everything happens for a reason. At least it was quick. It must have been their time. People mean well. They want to say something, anything, to fill a silence that feels unbearable. Back in year two, this path spent a run of days in the book of Job. Today it comes back with one question only: what does Job teach about being there for someone who's suffering? Today: Job again.

Start with what the friends got right. They came. In the King James Bible: "So they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great." Some readers say the friends never comforted Job better than in that week, and it was silent. Then they started talking. Their long speeches circle one idea: God is just, so if you're suffering, you must have done something. Job's reply is sharp: "miserable comforters are ye all." And he has already told them what would actually help: "O that ye would altogether hold your peace! and it should be your wisdom." Silence would have been the wise thing. Then God speaks, out of the whirlwind. You'd expect the explanation at last: the scene in heaven from the first chapter, the reason for it all. God never mentions it. Instead God asks Job questions. "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?" It isn't an answer. It's an encounter. Job, who demanded a hearing, gets one, and he goes quiet. Last, the rebuke. God turns to Eliphaz, one of the friends: "ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath." The friends with their tidy explanations are the ones corrected. Job, who wept and argued and accused, is the one said to have spoken rightly. Some readers notice the shape of the whole book. God didn't explain, but showed up. The friends explained, and were rebuked. That's where today's line comes from: show up, don't explain. It's harder than it sounds. Explaining feels like helping. Read this way, the book suggests that sitting on the ground beside someone, saying nothing, may be the more faithful thing.

Here's the practice: show up for someone. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone going through something hard right now. See their face. Notice any urge to fix it, to find the reason, to come up with the perfect sentence. Set it down. Now choose one way to simply be there: a visit, a meal left at the door, a message that says only I'm thinking of you, an hour beside them with no need to fill the quiet. If you pray, you can hold them before God without asking for an explanation. If you don't, hold them in mind, the way the friends sat on the ground. The bell holds the time.
Job again. The book of Job read for one lesson: God shows up without explaining, and the explaining friends are rebuked.
Your line: show up, don't explain. Today, do the one thing you chose for the person you thought of, and say less than you want to. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Job when they or someone close to them is suffering, and some pastors and chaplains point to the friends' silent week, and their later rebuke, as a pattern for visiting the grieving: be present, and resist explaining.

myth: Job tells his friends that holding their peace would be wisdom
"O that ye would altogether hold your peace! and it should be your wisdom."
Job finds his friends' speeches a great comfort
in the end, God says the friends spoke rightly and Job did not
it's the other way round: the friends "have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath."

fork.setup: you're Job. you've lost almost everything, and you've demanded a hearing. now God answers out of the whirlwind. what do you hear?
options: the reason for it all: the scene in heaven from the first chapter.
questions about the making of the world.
that your friends were right about you.
fork.reveal: "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?" God never mentions the scene in heaven. no explanation, but an encounter.

original.note: Hebrew: Iyov, Job's name in the Hebrew Bible.

trapdoor: what you thought: Job is a book about being patient.
what it means: the friends explain and are rebuked; God doesn't explain, but shows up.
what a scholar hears: Job 42:7: the friends "have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath." the one who argued with God is the one who spoke rightly.

notes: Year two (days 442–449) walked through Job; this day avoids repeating those myths and forks and reads the whole book for one lesson about comforting the suffering.
Hook's 'casserole' platitudes are illustrative of common sayings, not attributed to any church.
The friends' speeches summarized as 'God is just, so if you're suffering you must have done something'; confirm this is fair to all three (and to Elihu, who is not mentioned).
